content: The Cuban government operates a national healthcare system, taking full fiscal and administrative responsibility for the health of its citizens. Private hospitals and clinics are not allowed. The current Minister of Public Health is José Ramón Balaguer. Before Spanish colonization, Cuba had its own traditional medicine system, with high-status practitioners known as Bohiques. After colonization, Cuban medicine adopted Spanish traditions influenced by Moorish, Greek, and Roman practices. Chinese medicine also played a role, with figures like 19th-century doctor Cham Bom Biam, known as El Medico Chino. Modern Western medicine has been practiced in Cuba since at least the early 19th century, with the first surgical clinic established in 1823. Notable Cuban doctors include Carlos Finlay, who identified how yellow fever spreads, contributing to its eradication during the U.S. occupation (1898–1902). By the 1950s, Cuba had some of the best health indicators in the Americas, with life expectancy and doctor-to-population ratios surpassing many European countries. However, healthcare access was unequal, with rural areas like Oriente suffering from poor conditions and only 8% of the rural population having access to healthcare. After the Revolution, the government prioritized universal healthcare. In 1960, Che Guevara outlined goals for preventive medicine and public health education. However, the exodus of nearly half of Cuba’s physicians to the U.S. left the country with only 3,000 doctors. The Ministry of Public Health began nationalizing and regionalizing medical services, and in 1976, healthcare was enshrined as a constitutional right. Cuba implemented universal vaccination programs in the 1960s, eradicating diseases like polio and rubella. However, economic hardships in the 1990s led to a resurgence of diseases like tuberculosis and hepatitis. Maternal and prenatal care programs significantly reduced infant mortality rates. In 2007, Cuba began computerizing healthcare systems, creating national networks for blood banks, nephrology, and medical imaging. The country is also developing a computerized health register and hospital management systems to maintain free, high-quality healthcare and boost research. Cuba’s healthcare system has faced material shortages due to the U.S. embargo and the loss of Soviet subsidies. Despite this, Cuba has achieved impressive health outcomes. According to the WHO, Cuba’s infant mortality rate is lower than that of the U.S., and life expectancy is comparable. Preventive care, free diagnostic tests, and hospital treatments are provided, but some items like outpatient drugs and medical devices are paid for by patients who can afford them. The state subsidizes these items to keep prices low. Cuba has the second-highest doctor-to-patient ratio in the world, with one doctor for every 170 residents. However, doctors earn low salaries, leading some to work in the tourism industry for higher pay. The economic downturn of the 1990s exacerbated healthcare challenges, and a black market for medical services emerged. Some doctors charge patients for quicker or better services, a practice dating back to the 1970s. Cuba has agreements with international organizations like WHO, UNICEF, and UNDP, and exports medical personnel to other countries. Cuban doctors have provided aid in 68 countries, including during the South Asian tsunami and the Pakistan earthquake. In exchange for subsidized oil, Cuba sends medical teams to Venezuela. The Operación Milagro program, a joint initiative with Venezuela, offers free eye surgeries to millions in Latin America and the Caribbean. Cuba also attracts health tourists, generating significant revenue. The country provides treatments for conditions like multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease, and retinitis pigmentosa. It also exports medical products like vaccines. Economic constraints have led Cuba to integrate alternative medicine into its healthcare system, including herbal remedies and acupuncture. Children are taught about medicinal plants in school, and Cuban biochemists have developed alternative medicines like PPG® for cholesterol reduction. Cuba’s healthcare system has been praised internationally for its focus on prevention and community-based care. Despite low spending per capita, health outcomes like life expectancy and infant mortality rival those of developed nations. However, challenges remain, including low doctor salaries, outdated facilities, and shortages of equipment and essential drugs.
